source: Hu, Cheng, Chiu, Paller (2020) Promoting memory consolidation during sleep: meta-analysis of TMR
finding: First meta-analysis of sleep TMR. Overall benefit is small to moderate. Works in NREM, not in REM or wake.
numbers: 91 experiments, 212 effect sizes, N=2004. Overall Hedges g=0.29 [0.21,0.38]. N2 g=0.32 [0.04,0.60]. SWS g=0.27 [0.20,0.35]. REM and wake not effective. Several publication-bias checks run.
quote: TMR was not effective during REM sleep nor during wakefulness
limits: Abstract only read (full text blocked by bot check). Moderator details not verified.
agent_relevance: Replay is causal but the lever is small. A scaffold cue should be expected to give a modest gain, and only in the right state.

source: Rasch, Buchel, Gais, Born (2007) Odor cues during slow-wave sleep prompt declarative memory consolidation
finding: Rose odor present during learning, re-presented in SWS, improved hippocampus-dependent recall. No effect in REM, wake, procedural task, or if odor absent at learning. fMRI showed hippocampal activation to odor in SWS.
numbers: Exact retention figures not verified this session. Hoffman et al. (2024) table lists the awake odor arm as N=18, 8 h, null.
quote: Odor re-exposure was ineffective during rapid eye movement sleep or wakefulness or when the odor had been omitted during prior learning.
limits: Abstract only. Small N. Single lab at the time.
agent_relevance: The founding causal demonstration, and it already shows state dependence: same cue, no effect awake or in REM. Cue must match the context present at encoding.

source: Rudoy, Voss, Westerberg, Paller (2009) Strengthening individual memories by reactivating them during sleep
finding: Sounds linked to object locations were replayed during sleep. Cued locations were recalled more accurately than uncued ones. Effect is item-specific.
numbers: Hoffman et al. table lists the matching wake test as N=12, null.
quote: Consolidation thus operates during sleep with high specificity
limits: Abstract only. Small N. Nap, short delay.
agent_relevance: Shows item-level selectivity: the cue picks out single memories. Scaffold analogue is cueing one named sub-result, not the whole context.

source: Hoffman, Foley, Tanriverdi, Chein, Olson (2024) Awake targeted memory reactivation doesn't work
finding: Three experiments tested TMR while awake with Japanese vocabulary and Tetris as distractor. Cueing disrupted memory in Exp 1 and did nothing in Exp 2 and 3.
numbers: Final N=40, 40 and 41. Exp 2 raised study repeats from 3 to 6 to strengthen traces: still no benefit.
quote: awake TMR is not beneficial, and may actually impair subsequent memory
limits: Vocabulary only, auditory cues, one lab.
agent_relevance: State matters: the same cue that helps in NREM does nothing or harms while awake. Do not expect an in-context cue to act like a sleep cue.

source: Hoffman et al. (2024), literature table of awake TMR studies
finding: Table of 14 awake TMR results: mostly null. Positive: Farthouat 2017 (word pairs, N=41), Oudiette 2013 one condition, Salfi 2019 (N=39), Tambini 2017 (N=23, visual cue). Negative: Diekelmann 2011, Lehmann 2016.
numbers: Null results: Antony 2012 N=16, Cousins 2014 N=16, Rasch 2007 N=18, Rudoy 2009 N=12, Schreiner and Rasch 2015 N=34 and N=32, Schonauer 2014 N=29.
limits: Small samples throughout. Vote count, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Wake cueing is a weak lever. The positives involve brief cues and rest, not busy tasks.

source: Hoffman et al. (2024) rationale on encoding strength
finding: Authors note sleep TMR effects are largest for weakly encoded items (Cairney 2016; Creery 2015). They tried to boost encoding in Exp 2 and still found no wake effect.
numbers: Cites Hu 2020: TMR effects are not always observed.
limits: Narrative statement inside one paper.
agent_relevance: Cue only what is partly, not fully, learned. A well-solved subgoal gains nothing from reminders.

source: Wick and Rasch (2023) TMR during SWS vs N2: no significant differences in a vocabulary task
finding: Failed to find any overall benefit of cued over uncued Dutch-German words, and no difference between N2 and SWS cueing. N2 cues gave stronger theta and spindle responses that did not track memory.
numbers: Main sample 21 (8 h sleep) plus 13 (3 h). 120 word pairs, 40 uncued. 34 total.
quote: Our results question the robustness and replicability of the TMR benefit on memory using our Dutch vocabulary learning task.
limits: Underpowered. Authors call for multi-lab, larger replications.
agent_relevance: Even a canonical paradigm in a leading lab can fail. Treat single-lab TMR effects as fragile.

source: N2 vs SWS cueing with sound-word associations (Sci Rep, 2024; authors not verified)
finding: Cues in SWS were not better than in stage 2. If anything stage 2 was slightly better.
numbers: N=20 final. F(1,18)=4.05, p=0.059 for stage effect. Bayesian BF01=11.06 favouring equal effect. Power 0.83 for effect size 0.6.
limits: Within-subject, one cycle of sleep, 30 items.
agent_relevance: The deep-sleep requirement is looser than theory said. Light sleep also works.

source: theta-tACS coupled to TMR (2024) No benefit in memory after nocturnal memory reactivation coupled with theta-tACS
finding: Theta tACS during cueing did not help, and both tACS protocols blocked the usual TMR benefit.
limits: No TMR memory enhancement in either theta or control condition.
agent_relevance: Adding a second intervention on top of a cue can cancel it. Stack scaffold operators with care.

source: SleepStim (2022) Improving memory via automated TMR during sleep
finding: Home automated TMR with smartwatch. Exp 1 (N=61) showed no overall TMR effect but it varied with sound intensity: low-intensity helped, high-intensity did not. Exp 2 (N=24) with limited intensity gave a reliable benefit.
numbers: Cues in N3: 34.7% vs 21.1% base rate. 65.5% in N2 or N3. 13% of 120 participants heard a sound. Exp 1 bedtime error did not differ cued vs uncued (p=0.42).
quote: avoiding sleep disruption is critical for TMR benefits
limits: Object-location task over 3 nights. Exp 2 smaller.
agent_relevance: Cue intensity is a boundary condition: loud cues wake the sleeper and cancel the gain. Avoid disruptive reminders.

source: Face-name TMR (2022) TMR of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep
finding: Overall cued vs uncued difference was null, but the cueing benefit tracked N3 duration and was reduced by cue-related arousals.
numbers: N=24 (23 for recognition). Delta recall cued 0.75 vs uncued 0.21 items, t(23)=0.93, p=0.36. Cue effect vs N3 duration p=0.02; vs relative N3 p<0.001 (FDR 0.001). Recognition d' change 0.37 vs 0.49, p=0.22.
limits: Nap study, 80 face-name pairs, exploratory correlations.
agent_relevance: A moderator hides the effect in group means. Report effect by state quality, not by average.

source: Emotional arousal modulates oscillatory correlates of TMR (Sci Rep, 2016; authors not verified)
finding: Auditory cueing helped only in NREM, not REM or wake. Benefit was for emotionally arousing associations, not neutral ones.
numbers: N=62: NREM 21, REM 20, wake 21. NREM cueing benefit P=0.032, REM P=0.982, wake P=0.692. Group x valence F(1,59)=3.17, P=0.049. NREM vs wake for emotional items t=2.95, P=0.005. Neutral items: no benefit in any group (P>=0.26).
limits: Between-subject design.
agent_relevance: Cueing is selective for salient content. Replay priorities depend on arousal and value.

source: Schreiner et al. (2021) Endogenous memory reactivation during sleep in humans is clocked by slow oscillation-spindle complexes
finding: Without any external cue, EEG decoding finds reactivation during SO-spindle coupling. Stronger reactivation predicts better consolidation across people.
numbers: Nap paradigm, multivariate decoding of surface EEG. Participant count not extracted.
limits: Correlational across participants.
agent_relevance: Supports replay as a measurable event. Spontaneous replay, not only cued, tracks retention.

source: Closed-loop TMR for vocabulary at home with Dreem 2 headband (2025)
finding: Cues sent after real-time slow-wave detection raised recall of Italian words for pseudowords. Spindle power after the second slow-wave peak marked success.
numbers: N=24. Cued +8.6%, uncued -4.6%.
limits: Small N, no separate control group, uncued items slightly worsened.
agent_relevance: Timing cues to the right internal state gives the gain. Analogue: trigger a reminder when the agent is at a stable decision point.

source: Creery, Oudiette, Antony, Paller (2015) TMR during sleep depends on prior learning
finding: Cueing helped location recall in a nap, but only when pre-sleep accuracy was not near perfect. Benefit larger for people with higher pre-sleep recall.
numbers: N=20. Cue benefit correlated with delta power and fast spindle density.
limits: Abstract only. Authors inferred from title.
agent_relevance: Gain depends on a partly learned trace. Skip cueing items already mastered.

source: Oudiette, Antony, Creery, Paller (2013) review of reactivation during wakefulness and sleep
finding: Review of covert cueing by sound or odor. Cueing can help in sleep and sometimes awake; low-value items saved by cueing.
numbers: Hoffman table: N=30, mixed results by condition (null in one, positive in other).
limits: Abstract only for the related review.
agent_relevance: Value of the item changes whether cueing matters: low-value items benefit more.

source: Hauner, Howard, Zelano, Gottfried (2013) Stimulus-specific enhancement of fear extinction during slow-wave sleep
finding: Odor context present during fear conditioning was re-presented in SWS. This promoted stimulus-specific fear extinction with lowered hippocampal activity and amygdala pattern reorganization.
numbers: Numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Fear results are mixed elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Cueing can edit, not only strengthen, memory. A scaffold cue could weaken a bad prior.

source: Mouse V1 engram study (2021) Causal role for sleep-dependent reactivation of learning-activated sensory ensembles for fear memory
finding: Optogenetically inhibiting cue-responsive V1 neurons during post-conditioning sleep disrupted fear memory consolidation. Mimicking reactivation increased cue representation.
numbers: Counts not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Mouse.
agent_relevance: Closest causal test of necessity, not only sufficiency, of replay.

source: Dog TMR study (2025) The effect of TMR on dogs' visuospatial memory
finding: No cueing benefit on choice performance. Choice latency fell after sleep and fast spindle density was higher on TMR recordings.
numbers: N=16 dogs.
limits: Abstract only. Null behavior.
agent_relevance: A cross-species null: cue effects are not universal.

source: Odor-cued TMR unable to selectively benefit declarative memories (2026)
finding: Odor cueing during NREM gave no overall benefit for cued set. Effect depended on encoding strength. Odor induced about 15 s of sustained spectral inhibition, not a sigma increase.
numbers: N=32 (18 women, 14 men).
limits: Abstract only. Hierarchical context design.
agent_relevance: Cue effects may spread over the whole learning context. A cue may lift a whole cluster, not one item.

source: TMR cued once or five times during a nap (2025)
finding: No cue benefit whether sounds were played once or five times. Interference task raised error rates. Sigma power predicted gains for 5x cues only.
numbers: N=31, 60 object-sound pairs, 40 cued (20 once, 20 five times).
limits: Abstract only. Interference task may have swamped the effect.
agent_relevance: More repetitions of a cue do not simply add up. Dose-response is unresolved.

source: Difficulty in artificial word learning impacts TMR (2024)
finding: TMR helped easy-to-learn words but not difficult ones. Spindle power nested in slow-wave up states was higher for easy words.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Encoding depth gates replay. Poorly encoded material cannot be rescued by cueing.

source: Memory reactivation during sleep does not act holistically on object memory (2024)
finding: Real-time EEG cueing improved memory for distinguishing features and worsened shared features. A differentiation, not blanket gain.
numbers: N=34 (20 female, 14 male).
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Replay reshapes memory, it does not just boost it. A cue can sharpen differences and blur commonalities.

source: Emotional memory consolidation in SWS and REM with TMR (2025)
finding: Cueing emotional items in REM impaired memory. SWS benefit correlated with time in REM times SWS. Emotional memories gained more than neutral.
numbers: Numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Contradicts the older idea that REM cueing helps.
agent_relevance: State sign matters: the same cue can help in one stage and hurt in another.

source: Imagery rescripting plus closed-loop TMR at home (2024)
finding: Cueing words from the rescripted memory made memories less vivid and less distressing than rescripting alone.
numbers: N=80 across experimental and control groups. Imagery rescripting effect d=0.76-1.66.
limits: Abstract only. Clinical, mixed outcomes.
agent_relevance: Cue paired with an updated version of a memory can reinforce the updated version.

source: Tadros, Krishnan, Ramyaa, Bazhenov (2022) Sleep-like unsupervised replay reduces catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks
finding: An off-line sleep phase with local Hebbian updates and noisy input recovered old tasks that incremental training had made the network forget. Old-task activity rose and new-task activity fell.
numbers: Numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Neural networks, not an LLM. No external targeted cue.
agent_relevance: Closest AI analogue: offline replay works. It does not test a cue-selected replay, so no direct TMR test in an LLM was found.

source: Search note for this subfield (negative result)
finding: Searches (Europe PMC, arXiv) found no study that tests targeted memory reactivation as cueing of a language model. Cited AI work is general replay, not TMR.
numbers: 0 LLM TMR studies found. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate limited. WebSearch budget exhausted.
limits: Absence of evidence from limited search, not proof.
agent_relevance: Any TMR-style cue in the schema should be framed as untested by LLM evidence.
